first.rationale: Two candidate responses dominate: match the competitor with promotional pricing (memory_73) or fix the observed funnel decay via onboarding/activation (memory_86, memory_31, memory_91). Verification capacity goes to the two beliefs that are both decision-critical and weakest against the stated objective. memory_73 is the most consequential and most suspect: it reports acquisition and revenue lift, which are exactly the metrics that can look strong while eroding sustainable long-term qualified revenue through discount-anchored, price-shopping cohorts, margin compression, and renewal-time cliffs; the archived record needs to show whether retention, expansion, and post-discount revenue were ever measured or whether only top-of-funnel lift was observed. memory_86 is the belief my intended action rests on, and it is supported only by proxy metrics (completion rate, time-to-value, 'early product adoption') rather than qualified revenue; shortening onboarding can raise completion by removing qualification and configuration steps that are precisely what makes an account durable, so I need to know whether the original test tracked downstream revenue or only funnel proxies. I do not verify memory_31 (overlaps memory_86 and is the older, narrower version), memory_91 (activation messaging is lower-commitment and reversible, and its proxy-only support is less costly to be wrong about), or memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist does not address the SMB-side declines driving this quarter). Intended action: simplify_onboarding, because onboarding completion is down 4% and activation is down 6%, and the onboarding step sits upstream of the activation decline, so a single intervention there plausibly addresses both observed symptoms rather than buying volume that masks them. I run it as a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout for three reasons: the supporting evidence is proxy-metric evidence not revenue evidence; the day-52 result may not transfer to a market where a competitor has changed the mix of incoming accounts; and 'shorter onboarding' can improve completion while degrading cohort quality, which is the failure mode this objective most cares about. Guardrails should include 30/90-day retention, first-renewal rate, and revenue per activated account, not just completion. If the archive shows memory_86 was validated on revenue rather than completion, I would escalate scale; if it shows memory_73 tracked post-discount retention and held up, promotional_pricing becomes a live contender for the slot despite my prior. Remaining uncertainty is genuine: the QoQ declines could be caused by the competitor shifting inbound mix rather than by any onboarding regression, in which case a funnel fix treats a symptom of a demand-side change.

final.rationale: The archive resolved both questions in the direction that matters. exp_73 is disqualifying for the stated objective: +31% signup and +18% qualified revenue were accompanied by -12% 30-day retention, and the original record explicitly concludes the discounted cohort does not survive the first renewal cycle and should not be generalized as sustainable growth. The inherited summary of memory_73 ('strong acquisition and revenue lift') had silently dropped the retention harm, which is exactly the failure mode I was worried about: a belief that looks like a revenue win because only the favorable half of the result was carried forward. Promotional_pricing is therefore off the table for this slot, notwithstanding the competitor's entry pricing; matching a discount would buy volume that churns before it becomes qualified revenue, which is the opposite of the primary objective. memory_73 should be corrected in durable memory to carry the retention figure and the original 'do not generalize' caveat. exp_86 came back with more support than the summary implied: alongside completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention was +3%. That matters because my main reservation was that shortening onboarding might raise completion by stripping out qualification and configuration steps that make accounts durable. A positive retention signal is direct evidence against that failure mode, not just a proxy. Combined with the fact that onboarding completion is down 4% and sits upstream of the 6% activation decline, simplify_onboarding is the one intervention that plausibly addresses both observed symptoms while pointing at durable rather than borrowed revenue. I move from small_guarded_test to standard_experiment because the specific risk that justified the guard has been checked and did not materialize. I do not go to broad_rollout: exp_86 measured retention at 30 days, not renewal-cycle revenue or expansion, so the evidence supports durability over one month rather than over a renewal horizon, and the day-52 result was obtained before the competitor changed the composition of inbound SMB accounts. Run with retention, first-renewal rate, and revenue per activated account as tracked guardrails alongside completion, so this experiment produces the revenue-horizon evidence exp_86 lacks rather than another proxy-only record. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving this week: the QoQ declines may be partly driven by the competitor shifting inbound mix rather than by an onboarding regression, in which case a funnel fix improves conversion of a weaker pool and the underlying demand-side problem persists. activation_messaging (memory_91) remains an unverified proxy-only belief and is the natural next slot if onboarding underdelivers; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is unverified and does not address the SMB-side declines driving this quarter.
